entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Josh.18.1">Jos 18:1</reference> <div eID="gen2915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2916" type="x-p"/> The Tabernacle Set Up at Shiloh. - As soon as the tribe of Ephraim had received its inheritance, Joshua commanded the whole congregation to assemble in Shiloh, and there set up the tabernacle, in order that, as the land was conquered, the worship of Jehovah might henceforth be regularly observed in accordance with the law. The selection of Shiloh as the site for the sanctuary was hardly occasioned by the fitness of the place for this purpose, on account of its being situated upon a mountain in the centre of the land, for there were many other places that would have been quite as suitable in this respect; the reason is rather to be found in the name of the place, viz., <hi type="italic">Shiloh</hi>, i.e., rest, which called to mind the promised Shiloh (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen 49:10</reference>), and therefore appeared to be pre-eminently suitable to be the resting-place of the sanctuary of the Lord, where His name was to dwell in Israel, until He should come who was to give true rest to His people as the Prince of Peace. In any case, however, Joshua did not follow his own judgment in selecting Shiloh for this purpose, but acted in simple accordance with the instructions of God, as the Lord had expressly reserved to himself the choice of the place where His name should dwell (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.11">Deu 12:11</reference>). <hi type="italic">Shiloh</hi>, according to the <hi type="italic">Onom.</hi>, was twelve Roman miles or five hours to the south of Neapolis (Nablus), and about eight hours to the north of Jerusalem; at present it is a heap of ruins, bearing the name of <hi type="italic">Seilun</hi> (see <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> iii. p. 85). The tabernacle continued standing at Shiloh during the time of the judges, until the ark of the covenant fell into the hands of the Philistines, in the lifetime of Eli, when the holy tent was robbed of its soul, and reduced to the mere shadow of a sanctuary. After this it was removed to Nob (<reference osisRef="1Sam.21.2">1Sa 21:2</reference>); but in consequence of the massacre inflicted by Saul upon the inhabitants of this place (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.19">1Sa 22:19</reference>), it was taken to Gibeon (1Ki 3:4 : see <hi type="italic">Keil</hi>, Bibl. Arch. i. §22). From this time forward Shilloh continued to decline, because the Lord had rejected it (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.60">Psa 78:60</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.12">Jer 7:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.26.6">Jer 26:6</reference>). That it was destroyed by the Assyrians, as <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> affirms, is not stated in the history.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Josh.18.2">Jos 18:2</reference> <div eID="gen2916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2917" type="x-p"/> Survey of the Land that had yet to be Divided. - Jos 18:2. After the tabernacle had been set up, the casting of the lots and division of the land among the other seven tribes were to be continued; namely at Shiloh, to which the congregation had removed with the sanctuary.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Josh.18.3-Josh.18.4">Jos 18:3-4</reference> <div eID="gen2917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2918" type="x-p"/> But, for the reasons explained in <reference osisRef="Josh.14.1">Jos 14:1</reference>, these tribes showed themselves “<hi type="italic">slack to go to possess the land which the Lord had given them</hi>,” i.e., not merely to conquer it, but to have it divided by lot, and to enter in and take possession. Joshua charged them with this, and directed them to appoint three men for each of the seven tribes, that they might be sent out to go through the land, and describe it according to the measure of their inheritance. “<hi type="italic">According to their inheritance</hi>,” i.e., with special reference to the fact that seven tribes were to receive it for their inheritance. The description was not a formal measurement, although the art of surveying was well known in Egypt in ancient times, and was regularly carried out after the annual inundations of the Nile (<hi type="italic">Herod.</hi> ii. 109; <hi type="italic">Strabo</hi>, xvii. 787; <hi type="italic">Diod. Sic.</hi> i. 69); so that the Israelites might have learned it there. But כּתב does not mean to measure; and it was not a formal measurement that was required, for the purpose of dividing the land that yet remained into seven districts, since the tribes differed in numerical strength, and therefore the boundaries of the territory assigned them could not be settled till after the lots had been cast. The meaning of the word is to describe; and according to <reference osisRef="Josh.18.9">Jos 18:9</reference>, it was chiefly to the towns that reference was made: so that the description required by Joshua in all probability consisted simply in the preparation of lists of the towns in the different parts of the land, with an account of their size and character; also with “notices of the quality and condition of the soil; what lands were fertile, and what they produced; where the country was mountainous, and where it was level; which lands were well watered, and which were dry; and any other things that would indicate the character of the soil, and facilitate a comparison between the different parts of the land” (<hi type="italic">Rosenmüller</hi>). The reasons which induced Joshua to take steps for the first time now for securing a survey of the land, are given in Jos 14:1. The men chosen for the purpose were able to carry out their task without receiving any hindrance from the Canaanites. For whilst the latter were crushed, if not exterminated, by the victories which the Israelites had gained, it was not necessary for the twenty-one Israelitish men to penetrate into every corner of the land, and every town that was still inhabited by the Canaanites, in order to accomplish their end.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Josh.18.5-Josh.18.6">Jos 18:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen2918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2919" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And divide it into seven parts</hi>,” viz., for the purpose of casting lots. Judah, however, was still to remain in its land to the south, and Ephraim in its territory to the north. The seven portions thus obtained they were to bring to Joshua, that he might then cast the lot for the seven tribes “before the Lord,” i.e., before the tabernacle (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.51">Jos 19:51</reference>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Josh.18.12-Josh.18.14">Jos 18:12-14</reference> <div eID="gen2923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2924" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">northern boundary</hi> (“the boundary towards the north side”) therefore coincided with the southern boundary of Ephraim as far as Lower Beth-horon, and has already been commented upon in the exposition of <reference osisRef="Josh.16.1">Jos 16:1</reference>-3. The <hi type="italic">western boundary</hi> follows in Jos 18:14. At Beth-horon the boundary curved round and turned southwards on the western side, namely from the mountain before (in front of) Beth-horon southwards; and “<hi type="italic">the going out thereof were at Kirjath-baal, which is Kirjath-jearim</hi>,” the town of the Judaeans mentioned in <reference osisRef="Josh.15.60">Jos 15:60</reference>, the present <hi type="italic">Kureyet el Enab</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.9.17">Jos 9:17</reference>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Josh.18.15-Josh.18.19">Jos 18:15-19</reference> <div eID="gen2924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2925" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">As for the southern boundary from the end of Kirjath-jearim onwards, the</hi> (southern) <hi type="italic">boundary went out on the west</hi> (i.e., it started from the west), <hi type="italic">and went out</hi> (terminated) <hi type="italic">at the fountain of the water of Nephtoah</hi>.” Consequently it coincided with the northern boundary of Judah, as described in <reference osisRef="Josh.15.5-Josh.15.9">Jos 15:5-9</reference>, except that it is given there from east to west, and here from west to east (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.15.5-Josh.15.9">Jos 15:5-9</reference>). In the construction haגּבוּל תּוצאותיו, the noun הגּבוּל is in apposition to the suffix: the outgoings of it, namely of the border (see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §291, <hi type="italic">b</hi>.).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Josh.18.21-Josh.18.28">Jos 18:21-28</reference> <div eID="gen2926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2927" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">towns</hi> of Benjamin are divided into two groups. The <hi type="italic">first</hi> group (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.21-Josh.18.24">Jos 18:21-24</reference>) contains twelve towns in the eastern portion of the territory. <hi type="italic">Jericho</hi>: the present <hi type="italic">Riha</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.2.1">Jos 2:1</reference>). <hi type="italic">Beth-hoglah</hi>, now <hi type="italic">Ain Hajla</hi> (see <reference osisRef="Josh.15.6">Jos 15:6</reference>). <hi type="italic">Emek-keziz</hi>: the name has been preserved in the Wady <hi type="italic">el Kaziz</hi>, on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho, on the south-east of the Apostle’s Well (see <hi type="italic">Van de Velde</hi>, Mem. p. 328).
